tagline: A former forest motorway follows Alabama’s highest range to Adams Gap
intro: Talladega Scenic Drive follows the crest of Alabama’s highest mountain range on State Route 281. The Forest Service presents the drive as 29 miles of mountain and national-forest views, winding along the southern Appalachians. Cheaha State Park provides access to the state’s highest natural point. The mountain’s stone observation tower looks south across second-growth woodland into Cheaha Wilderness.

Before the pavement, this was the Skyway Motorway, an unpaved forest route. The scenic drive initially carried the numbers SR 49 and SR 49 Spur. The earlier spur climbed to Cheaha Mountain, then continued west toward Talladega as a narrow county road. In the early 1990s, the spur was extended south along the mountains’ western side to a fork of forest roads. After that work, the spur and the section of SR 49 north of it became SR 281.

Start west of Heflin at US 78 and follow SR 281 toward Cheaha. The road crosses US 431 and I-20 on overpasses without interchanges. At Cheaha, Bunker Tower and Bald Rock offer overlooks. Cheaha Wilderness lies within Talladega National Forest, beside the state park; Congress designated it in 1983 and expanded it in 1988. Continue south toward Adams Gap, where the scenic drive’s pavement ends at Forest Service Road 600.

moments.title: Cheaha Mountain
moments.text: Alabama’s highest natural point is marked by a USGS benchmark in front of Bunker Tower. The Civilian Conservation Corps completed this native rubble-stone observation tower in 1934. Its first-floor wings originally held park offices and a gift shop. The CCC’s work extended across the park: crews created Cheaha Lake and built stone cabins, pavilions and hiking trails between 1933 and 1939. From the summit tower, second-growth woodland extends south into Cheaha Wilderness. A tall Alabama Public Television transmitter stands immediately beside the stone tower, another landmark among the trees at the summit.

moments.title: Bald Rock
moments.text: A wooden walkway on the Bald Rock Trail leads to an overlook of the surrounding region. On January 4, 1944, a P-38 Lightning flying from Dallas to Atlanta crashed into Bald Rock. Its pilot was 2nd Lieutenant Chester R. Gunkel of Milwaukee. A machine gun recovered from the crash site was donated to the park museum in 2023.

moments.title: Adams Gap
moments.text: At Adams Gap, the pavement ends at Forest Service Road 600. The southern highway extension reached a fork of two forest roads in the early 1990s; one belonged to the old Skyway Motorway. The route’s unusual mileposts reflect an unfinished measurement: ALDOT uses Mile 500 as a countdown because the highway’s eventual length is unknown. Those high numbers do not establish that a longer road was always planned.

practical: Adams Gap: The paved scenic drive ends at Adams Gap and Forest Service Road 600. (checked 2026-10-11)
